**Summary.** Most of Myanmar's armed conflict since the 2021 coup happened in the central Dry Zone. A block of townships in Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay was a hot spot in almost every quarter. The conflict did not leave this core. It spread out from it, into Bago, along the road to northern Shan, into central Rakhine and down to the far south. Yangon and the Ayeyarwady delta became steadily quieter. The military's air strikes rose about 23-fold, and rose most in the Dry Zone and on the new fronts. Two bonus analyses add detail. The first finds townships in Yangon and around Mandalay city with few battles but many bombs and attacks on civilians, which maps of total counts do not show. The second groups neighbouring townships into eight regions whose conflict rose and fell at the same time.

The task is set out in the [Take-home Exercise 2 brief](https://isss626-ay2026-27aug.netlify.app/take-home_ex02). The Executive Summary is [here](Take-home_Ex02_slides.html).

# Introduction

In February 2021 Myanmar's military seized power from the elected government. Peaceful protests were met with force, and many people took up arms. By 2023 large parts of the country had slipped out of the junta's control, and more than three million people had fled their homes (ACLED, 2024; CFR, 2025).

The violence is uneven. Some townships see fighting every week and others see almost none. People planning aid, protecting civilians or monitoring a ceasefire need to know where the violence is concentrated and where it is heading.

This report looks at both, township by township, from January 2021 to September 2025. Local measures of spatial association find where conflict clusters and which townships stand out. Emerging hot spot analysis shows how those clusters grew, faded or moved. Mack and Kam (2018) used the same kind of space-time analysis on conflict data.

# Research Question and Objectives

**Research question.** Where does armed conflict in Myanmar cluster, and how have these clusters changed since the 2021 coup?

The brief sets two objectives. They lead to five questions, each answered in one part of the report.

| Brief objective | Question | Part | Main method |
|---|---|---|---|
| (Groundwork) | Q1. Where and when did armed conflict happen? | Task 1 | Choropleth maps, small multiples, time series |
| 1. Hot spots, cold spots and outliers | Q2. Where does conflict cluster, and which townships stand out from their neighbours? | Task 2 | Local Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi\* |
| 2. Where, how fast and in what pattern violence evolves | Q3. Where are hot and cold spots emerging, growing or fading? | Task 3 | Mann-Kendall test, emerging hot spot analysis |
| 1, extended to the kind of violence | Q4. Do neighbouring townships face the same *kind* of violence, and where does the mix stand out? | Bonus 1 | Multivariate local Geary's c |
| 2, extended from townships to regions | Q5. Which neighbouring townships went through the same timeline of conflict? | Bonus 2 | SKATER spatially constrained clustering |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,10,28]"}

Q4 is asked because a township hit by air strikes and one hit by ground battles need different help, even when their totals are the same. Q5 is asked because aid and ceasefire monitoring are planned by area, and two neighbouring townships with the same EHSA label can have had their worst fighting years apart.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Five terms used throughout
- **Event**. One ACLED record of armed conflict, such as a clash, an air strike or an attack on civilians.
- **Neighbours**. The 8 townships whose centres are nearest to a township. Every local statistic compares a township with these neighbours.
- **Null model**. What the map would look like if the same values were shuffled at random across townships. Every result is judged against it.
- **Significant**. A result that random shuffling would produce less than 5 times in 100 (p < 0.05).
- **Hot spot**. A township whose neighbourhood, including itself, has far more events than random shuffling would give. A cold spot has far fewer.
:::

# Task 1. Geospatial Data Science

## Loading the Packages

`p_load()` from **pacman** loads the packages below and installs any that are missing. The workflow follows the course text (Kam, 2026d).

| Package | Job in this report |
|---|---|
| **sf** | Reads the township boundary, turns events into points, reprojects and joins them |
| **sfdep** | Neighbours, weights, local Moran's I, Gi\*, local Geary's c, the space-time cube and EHSA |
| **spdep** | Global Getis-Ord G, the neighbour summaries, the spatial correlogram and SKATER clustering |
| **tmap** | All other maps |
| **tidyverse** | Reading, filtering, counting, the charts and the year-by-year map |
| **Kendall** | The Mann-Kendall trend test |
| **modifiedmk** | A Mann-Kendall test corrected for serial correlation, used as a check |
| **knitr** | Tables |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, sfdep, spdep, tmap, tidyverse, Kendall, modifiedmk, knitr)
sf_use_s2(FALSE)   # planar geometry, since all work is in a projected CRS
```


## Data and Study Design

### The data

| Dataset | Source | Coverage used | What it holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| ACLED event data, Myanmar | Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, file provided on eLearn | 1 Jan 2021 to 30 Sep 2025, 87,109 events | One row per event, with date, type, actors, coordinates and precision codes |
| Myanmar Township Boundaries MIMU v9.4 | Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU) GeoNode, geonode.themimu.info, layer `mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1` | 330 townships | Polygons with MIMU place codes (`TS_PCODE`) for state, district and township |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,28,22,30]"}

The raw files are in `data/rawdata/acled` and `data/rawdata/mimu`. The code reads whatever shapefile is in the MIMU folder, so a newer boundary release can be used without changing the code.

### Study design

| Element | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Study area | All of Myanmar, 330 townships in 18 states and regions | Set by the brief |
| Unit | Township, matched on `TS_PCODE` | The brief's unit. Codes avoid spelling differences in names |
| Period | 1 Jan 2021 to 30 Sep 2025 | Set by the brief. It starts one month before the coup, as a baseline |
| Time step | Quarter, 19 steps | A month leaves most township bins at zero. A year gives only 5 points, too few for a trend test. The lecture notes ask for at least 8 to 10 |
| Variables | Counts of battles, explosions and remote violence, violence against civilians, and their total | The three ACLED types that are armed conflict |
| CRS | WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N, EPSG 32647 | Covers most of Myanmar, in metres. The far west is in zone 46, but neighbours are found by ranking distances, and the ranking hardly changes |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,32,52]"}

ACLED codes six event types (Raleigh et al., 2010). Only three are armed conflict.

| ACLED event type | Kept? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Battles | Yes | Armed clashes between organised groups |
| Explosions/Remote violence | Yes | Air strikes, drone strikes, shelling, landmines and bombs |
| Violence against civilians | Yes | Attacks, abductions and killings of unarmed people |
| Protests | No | Mostly peaceful, so not armed conflict |
| Riots | No | Mob violence rather than armed conflict |
| Strategic developments | No | Not violent events, such as arrests or base handovers |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,12,58]"}

## Data Preparation and Quality Assessment

The brief warns that data are like a grassland full of land mines. The table lists the ones found in these two files, in the order the steps below handle them.

| # | Land mine | Why it matters | What was done | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6 rows are not in Myanmar at all | They are incidents off the coast of India and Sri Lanka, filed under "Indian Ocean" | Keep only rows where `country` is Myanmar | 6 rows removed |
| 2 | Over a third of the file is not armed conflict | Protests and arrests would inflate the counts | Keep only the three conflict types | 54,000 events kept |
| 3 | 1,118 events have no township name, and others use names the boundary file does not have | A name join would drop or misplace them | Place every event by its coordinates | No event lost to names |
| 4 | 8 events fall just outside every township | They sit on the coastline, where the boundary is simplified | Snap them to the nearest township if within 5 km | All 8 snapped |
| 5 | Some events are placed only roughly | They could land in the wrong township | Count how many are placed only to a region | 93 events, too few to move any result |
| 6 | Some events are dated only to a week or month | They could fall in the wrong quarter | Count week-dated events near a quarter's edge | About 125, a fraction of one percent |
| 7 | "Air/drone strike" mixes military aircraft and resistance drones | One label hides two opposite sides of the war | Split by the actor who carried it out | Military air strikes analysed on their own |
| 8 | 8 townships have no event, and a third of township-quarters are empty | Dropping them would bias every statistic | Keep them as real zeros and fill every quarter | A complete space-time cube |
| 9 | sfdep's emerging hot spot function can attach results to the wrong township | The map would be wrong without any warning | Sort the boundary by township code before building the cube | Checked against an independent trend test |

: {tbl-colwidths="[5,24,25,24,22]"}

### Reading the township boundary

`st_read()` reads the MIMU shapefile. `st_make_valid()` repairs any broken polygons, and `st_transform()` moves the map to UTM 47N so that distances are in metres. The boundary is sorted by `TS_PCODE`, which land mine 9 needs.

```{r}
#| filename: "read, repair and reproject the townships"
mimu_file <- list.files("data/rawdata/mimu", pattern = "\\.shp$", full.names = TRUE)
mmr_ts <- st_read(mimu_file, quiet = TRUE)

tibble(file = basename(mimu_file), townships = nrow(mmr_ts),
       states_regions = n_distinct(mmr_ts$ST),
       invalid = sum(!st_is_valid(mmr_ts)),
       duplicate_codes = sum(duplicated(mmr_ts$TS_PCODE))) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("File", "Townships", "States and regions", "Invalid geometries", "Duplicate codes"))

mmr_ts <- mmr_ts %>%
  st_make_valid() %>%
  st_transform(32647) %>%
  select(ST, ST_PCODE, DT, TS, TS_PCODE) %>%
  arrange(TS_PCODE)

area_km2 <- as.numeric(st_area(mmr_ts)) / 1e6
```

The boundary has `r nrow(mmr_ts)` townships with unique codes. They range from `r round(min(area_km2), 1)` km² in central Yangon to `r format(round(max(area_km2)), big.mark = ",")` km² in Kachin. This large spread in size affects the choice of neighbours in Task 2.

### Reading and checking the ACLED events

`read_csv()` reads the file. Before any filtering, the raw file is checked for the problems most common in event data.

```{r}
#| filename: "read ACLED and check its quality"
acled_raw <- read_csv("data/rawdata/acled/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv")

tibble(
  check = c("Rows and columns", "First and last date", "Duplicate event IDs", "Missing coordinates",
            "No township name (admin3)", "Placed at the exact spot (geo precision 1)",
            "Placed at a nearby town (geo precision 2)", "Placed only to a region (geo precision 3)",
            "Dated only to a week or month (time precision 2 or 3)"),
  result = c(paste(format(nrow(acled_raw), big.mark = ","), "by", ncol(acled_raw)),
             paste(min(acled_raw$event_date), "to", max(acled_raw$event_date)),
             sum(duplicated(acled_raw$event_id_cnty)),
             sum(is.na(acled_raw$latitude) | is.na(acled_raw$longitude)),
             format(sum(is.na(acled_raw$admin3)), big.mark = ","),
             format(sum(acled_raw$geo_precision == 1), big.mark = ","),
             format(sum(acled_raw$geo_precision == 2), big.mark = ","),
             sum(acled_raw$geo_precision == 3),
             format(sum(acled_raw$time_precision > 1), big.mark = ","))
) %>% kable(col.names = c("Check", "Result"))
```

There are no duplicates, no missing coordinates and no dates outside the study period. The problems are about place and event type, starting with the `country` column.

```{r}
#| filename: "rows that are not in Myanmar"
acled_raw %>% count(country) %>% kable(col.names = c("Country", "Rows"))

acled_raw %>% filter(country != "Myanmar") %>%
  transmute(event_date, event_type, location, note = str_trunc(notes, 90)) %>% kable()
```

Six rows are filed under "Indian Ocean". Their notes show clashes involving Indian and Sri Lankan fishers and navies, far from Myanmar, placed in the middle of the Bay of Bengal. They are removed first. Otherwise the snapping step below would either move them onto the coast or drop them without comment.

### Keeping the armed conflict events (land mines 1, 2 and 7)

`filter()` keeps Myanmar's rows and the three conflict types. Two columns are added. `quarter` gives each event's quarter for the cube. `military_air` marks air and drone strikes by the military, because ACLED puts the military's aircraft and the resistance's drones under the same sub-type.

```{r}
#| filename: "keep the three conflict types and derive new columns"
conflict <- acled_raw %>%
  filter(country == "Myanmar",
         event_type %in% c("Battles", "Explosions/Remote violence", "Violence against civilians")) %>%
  mutate(type = recode(event_type, "Explosions/Remote violence" = "Explosions and remote violence"),
         quarter = paste0(year(event_date), "Q", quarter(event_date)),
         military_air = sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike" &
                        str_detect(coalesce(actor1, ""), "Military Forces of Myanmar"))

conflict %>% count(type) %>% mutate(share = scales::percent(n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Event type", "Events", "Share"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

conflict %>% filter(sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike") %>%
  count(year, by = if_else(military_air, "Military", "Resistance and other groups")) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = by, values_from = n) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Military", "Resistance and other groups"))
```

Explosions and remote violence is the largest type, ahead of battles. The second table shows why land mine 7 matters. Resistance drone strikes were more than half of all "air/drone strikes" in 2023 and then fell, while the military's air strikes kept rising.

### Placing events in townships (land mines 3 and 4)

`st_as_sf()` turns each event into a point, and `st_join()` with `st_within` gives it the township it falls in, so missing or mismatched names do not matter. For points outside every polygon, `st_nearest_feature()` finds the nearest township. Points within 5 km are coastal events and are snapped to it. Points further out would be dropped and listed.

```{r}
#| filename: "spatial join, with snapping for coastal events"
conflict_sf <- conflict %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(32647) %>%
  st_join(mmr_ts %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS), join = st_within)

miss <- which(is.na(conflict_sf$TS_PCODE))
near <- st_nearest_feature(conflict_sf[miss, ], mmr_ts)
gap_km <- as.numeric(st_distance(conflict_sf[miss, ], mmr_ts[near, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 1000
snap <- gap_km <= 5
conflict_sf$TS_PCODE[miss[snap]] <- mmr_ts$TS_PCODE[near[snap]]
conflict_sf$TS[miss[snap]]       <- mmr_ts$TS[near[snap]]

conflict_sf <- filter(conflict_sf, !is.na(TS_PCODE))
```

`r length(miss)` events fell just outside every township, the furthest `r round(max(gap_km), 1)` km from land, and `r sum(snap)` were snapped. None were dropped. All `r format(nrow(conflict_sf), big.mark = ",")` events now have a township.

The result is then compared with ACLED's own township names.

```{r}
#| filename: "ACLED names against the township each point falls in"
name_check <- conflict_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(admin3), str_to_lower(admin3) != str_to_lower(TS)) %>%
  count(admin3, TS, sort = TRUE)

name_check %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("ACLED township name", "Township the point falls in", "Events"))
```

`r format(sum(name_check$n), big.mark = ",")` events (`r round(100 * sum(name_check$n) / nrow(conflict_sf), 1)` percent) have an ACLED name that differs from the township their point falls in. Most are in townships that ACLED splits but the boundary file does not, such as Dagon Myothit and Hlaingtharya in Yangon. A join by name would have lost them.

### Checking place and date precision (land mines 5 and 6)

```{r}
#| filename: "region-level places and week-dated events near quarter edges"
edge_days <- conflict_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(time_precision == 2) %>%
  mutate(from_start = as.numeric(event_date - floor_date(event_date, "quarter")),
         to_end = as.numeric(ceiling_date(event_date, "quarter") - 1 - event_date))

tibble(check = c("Events placed only to a region", "Week-dated events within 3 days of a quarter's edge"),
       events = c(sum(conflict_sf$geo_precision == 3),
                  sum(edge_days$from_start < 3 | edge_days$to_end < 3)),
       share = scales::percent(events / nrow(conflict_sf), 0.1)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Check", "Events", "Share of all events"))
```

About `r round(100 * mean(conflict_sf$geo_precision == 2))` percent of the kept events are placed at a nearby town rather than the exact spot, which is close enough for township counts. The two risky groups are each well under one percent of events, so they are kept.

### Counting by township (land mine 8)

`count()` gives each township's events by type, and `pivot_wider()` turns the types into columns. Townships with no events get a zero, not a blank.

```{r}
#| filename: "township counts for the four conflict variables"
conflict_ts <- conflict_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(var = recode(type, "Battles" = "battles",
                      "Explosions and remote violence" = "remote",
                      "Violence against civilians" = "civilians")) %>%
  count(TS_PCODE, var) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = var, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(total = battles + remote + civilians)

mmr_conflict <- mmr_ts %>%
  left_join(conflict_ts, by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  mutate(across(c(battles, remote, civilians, total), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))

summary(mmr_conflict$total)
```

`r sum(mmr_conflict$total == 0)` townships recorded no armed conflict, and they stay in as zeros. The counts are very skewed. The median township had `r median(mmr_conflict$total)` events and the mean was `r round(mean(mmr_conflict$total))`, pulled up by a few townships with hundreds. This skew also affects the choice of neighbours in Task 2.

### Building the space-time cube

Events are counted for every township and quarter, for each conflict variable and for military air strikes. `complete()` fills empty township-quarters with zeros, so every township has all 19 quarters. `spacetime()` from **sfdep** links the counts to the township polygons, and `is_spacetime_cube()` confirms the cube is complete.

```{r}
#| filename: "space-time cube with all conflict variables"
quarters <- paste0(rep(2021:2025, each = 4), "Q", 1:4)[1:19]

cube_counts <- conflict_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(var = recode(type, "Battles" = "battles",
                      "Explosions and remote violence" = "remote",
                      "Violence against civilians" = "civilians")) %>%
  count(TS_PCODE, quarter, var) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = var, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  left_join(conflict_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(military_air) %>%
              count(TS_PCODE, quarter, name = "military_air"), by = c("TS_PCODE", "quarter")) %>%
  complete(TS_PCODE = mmr_ts$TS_PCODE, quarter = quarters,
           fill = list(battles = 0, remote = 0, civilians = 0, military_air = 0)) %>%
  mutate(military_air = replace_na(military_air, 0),
         total = battles + remote + civilians,
         time = match(quarter, quarters))

conflict_st <- spacetime(cube_counts, mmr_ts %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST),
                         .loc_col = "TS_PCODE", .time_col = "time")
is_spacetime_cube(conflict_st)
```

The cube has `r nrow(mmr_ts)` townships by 19 quarters, or `r format(nrow(cube_counts), big.mark = ",")` bins, each with five counts. `r round(100 * mean(cube_counts$total == 0))` percent of bins have no event.

```{r}
#| echo: false
dir.create("data/rds", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(list(mmr_conflict = mmr_conflict, cube_counts = cube_counts,
               events = conflict_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
                 select(TS_PCODE, year, quarter, type, sub_event_type, military_air)),
          "data/rds/prepared.rds")
```

## Where and When Conflict Happened

Five charts and maps answer Q1 before any statistics. They show where counts are high, how they changed over time, and why each type of violence is looked at separately.

Every map uses the same state borders and state names, so these layers are built once. A few names in the crowded south are moved slightly so they do not overlap. Each name sits on a pale box so it can be read on dark fills, and all map text is made 20 percent larger.

```{r}
#| filename: "shared map layers"
mmr_st <- mmr_ts %>% group_by(ST) %>% summarise()

nudge <- tribble(~ST, ~dx_km, ~dy_km,
  "Ayeyarwady", -45, -15,   "Yangon", 15, -40,      "Mon", -15, -45,
  "Bago (West)", -35, 25,   "Bago (East)", 30, -15, "Kayin", 45, 10,
  "Shan (South)", -25, 0,   "Shan (East)", 40, 0,   "Tanintharyi", 80, 0)

st_lab <- st_point_on_surface(mmr_st) %>%
  mutate(x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1], y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  left_join(nudge, by = "ST") %>%
  mutate(x = x + coalesce(dx_km, 0) * 1000, y = y + coalesce(dy_km, 0) * 1000) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = st_crs(mmr_st))

state_borders <- tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey20", lwd = 0.8)
state_names   <- tm_shape(st_lab) +
  tm_text("ST", size = 0.55, col = "grey5", bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.65)

# larger text on every map, and keep titles at full size instead of shrinking them to the map's width
tmap_options(scale = 1.2, component.autoscale = FALSE)
```

## Analytical Assumptions and Methodological Decisions

The maps above show counts that are skewed, uneven across townships and changing over time. The choices below take this into account. Each is explained again where it is used.

| Decision | Choice | Why | Risk, and how it is checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| Measure | Event counts, not rates | Counts are what the brief asks for, and no reliable township population for 2021 to 2025 is available | A busy town may look high because more happens there. Read with care |
| Neighbours | 8 nearest townships, by centre point | Townships range from under 1 km² to over 12,000 km², 3 are islands, and counts are skewed. The lecture notes advise about 8 neighbours in this case | Rural neighbours reach further than urban ones. Checked with queen contiguity |
| Weights | Row-standardised. The township itself is included for Gi\* | Standard for local Moran's I and Gi\* (Getis and Ord, 1992) | Every neighbour counts the same |
| Null model | Conditional permutation, 999 shuffles (199 in Task 3, explained there) | Makes no assumption that counts are normally distributed | Permutation p-values vary slightly by run, so the seed is fixed |
| Significance | p < 0.05. Two-sided for local Moran's I and Gi\*. EHSA uses sfdep's own per-quarter p-value | Set by the brief | With 330 tests some results are false alarms. Checked with the false discovery rate |
| Time step | Quarter | Enough events per bin, and 19 points for a trend test | Short bursts inside a quarter are smoothed |
| Trend test | Mann-Kendall on Gi\* | Set by the brief | It assumes no serial correlation, which conflict series break. Checked with a corrected test |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,26,30,30]"}

# Task 2. Local Measures of Spatial Association

Task 2 answers Q2 and the brief's first objective. It finds where conflict clusters and which townships are unlike their neighbours.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Short answer
Conflict is strongly clustered. A block of 28 Dry Zone townships forms the main High-High cluster, and a smaller one sits around Dawei in Tanintharyi. Low-Low clusters cover Yangon, the Ayeyarwady delta and eastern Shan. Gi\* finds 40 hot spots holding 31 percent of all events. No busy township sits alone among quiet neighbours. The 8 outliers are quieter townships at the edge of hot areas. A median split adds one borderline case, Thaketa in Yangon. Each type of violence clusters in the Dry Zone, and each has a different second cluster. The High-High core survives a false discovery rate correction and a different neighbour rule. The Low-Low areas shrink and most outliers change, so the outliers are the least certain result.
:::

## Step 1. Choosing the neighbours

Every local statistic compares a township with its neighbours, so this choice affects every result. Two rules are compared. `st_contiguity()` makes townships that share a border neighbours. `st_knn()` takes the 8 townships whose centre points are nearest, using `st_point_on_surface()` so that every point lies inside its own township.

```{r}
#| filename: "queen contiguity against 8 nearest neighbours"
centres  <- st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(mmr_conflict))
nb_queen <- st_contiguity(mmr_conflict, queen = TRUE)
nb_knn   <- st_knn(centres, k = 8)

nb_summary <- function(nb, rule) {
  n <- spdep::card(nb)
  tibble(rule = rule, min = min(n), median = median(n), max = max(n), no_neighbour = sum(n == 0),
         separate_groups = spdep::n.comp.nb(nb)$nc)
}
bind_rows(nb_summary(nb_queen, "Queen contiguity"), nb_summary(nb_knn, "8 nearest neighbours")) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Rule", "Fewest neighbours", "Median", "Most", "Townships with none", "Separate groups"))
```

Queen contiguity leaves `r sum(spdep::card(nb_queen) == 0)` island townships (`r paste(mmr_conflict$TS[spdep::card(nb_queen) == 0], collapse = ", ")`) with no neighbour, and breaks Myanmar into pieces that are not connected. Townships also vary greatly in size, and the counts are skewed. For this situation the Lesson 5 notes (Kam, 2026b) recommend nearest neighbours, about eight when values are skewed. So **8 nearest neighbours** are used throughout, and queen contiguity is used as a check in Step 6. Section 10.5.1.2 of the course text builds Gi\* weights the same way, `include_self(st_knn())` with row-standardised weights (Kam, 2026d).

```{r}
#| filename: "weights"
wm_knn <- mmr_conflict %>%
  mutate(nb = nb_knn, wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"), .before = 1)          # for local Moran's I
wm_gi  <- mmr_conflict %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(nb_knn), wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"), .before = 1)   # for Gi*, self included
```

## Step 2. Is there clustering at all?

Local statistics are only worth reading if the map is clustered overall. Lesson 5 gives three global measures for this. Global Moran's I compares each township with the national average and is above 0 when similar values are near each other. Global Geary's c compares each township directly with its neighbours and is below 1 when they are alike. Getis-Ord global G tests whether the *high* values are near each other, and uses binary weights, as its formula expects. The null model is 999 permutations, or the randomisation test for G.

```{r}
#| filename: "global Moran's I, Geary's c and G for the four variables"
var_names <- c(total = "Total", battles = "Battles", remote = "Explosions and remote violence",
               civilians = "Violence against civilians")
set.seed(1234)
global_tab <- map_dfr(names(var_names), function(v) {
  m <- global_moran_perm(wm_knn[[v]], wm_knn$nb, wm_knn$wt, nsim = 999, alternative = "greater")
  c <- global_c_perm(wm_knn[[v]], wm_knn$nb, wm_knn$wt, nsim = 999)
  g <- global_g_test(wm_knn[[v]], wm_knn$nb, st_weights(wm_knn$nb, style = "B"))
  tibble(variable = var_names[[v]], moran_i = round(m$statistic, 2),
         moran_p = sprintf("%.3f", m$p.value),
         geary_c = round(c$statistic, 2), geary_p = sprintf("%.3f", c$p.value),
         g_z = round(g$statistic[[1]], 1), g_p = format.pval(g$p.value, eps = 0.001, digits = 2))
})
global_tab %>% kable(col.names = c("Variable", "Moran's I", "p-value", "Geary's c", "p-value", "Global G, z", "p-value"))
```

::: {.read}
**All four variables are clearly clustered.** Moran's I is between `r sprintf('%.2f', min(global_tab$moran_i))` and `r sprintf('%.2f', max(global_tab$moran_i))`, and none of the 999 random shuffles came close. The null hypothesis of random placement is rejected for every variable (one-sided test for clustering, as in chapter 9 of the course text, p = 0.001, the smallest p-value 999 shuffles can give). Geary's c is between `r sprintf('%.2f', min(global_tab$geary_c))` and `r sprintf('%.2f', max(global_tab$geary_c))`, well below 1, so neighbouring townships are alike when compared directly. As the lecture notes say, a high Moran's I goes with a low Geary's c, and here they agree. Global G is strongly positive, with z-scores of `r floor(min(global_tab$g_z))` to `r ceiling(max(global_tab$g_z))`, so high counts in particular are near each other. The four variables give similar results, so no single type drives the pattern.
:::

### How far does the clustering reach?

The neighbour rule sets the scale of every local statistic, so it helps to know how far the clustering reaches. A spatial correlogram, `sp.correlogram()` from **spdep** as in chapter 9 of the course text, repeats Moran's I for neighbours of neighbours. Order 1 is the 8 nearest townships, order 2 adds their 8 nearest, and so on. The table also gives the typical distance between a township and its neighbours at each order.

```{r}
#| filename: "Moran's I correlogram over six orders of neighbours"
corr <- sp.correlogram(nb_knn, mmr_conflict$total, order = 6, method = "I", style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
lags <- nblag(nb_knn, 6)
corr_tab <- tibble(order = 1:6,
                   distance_km = map_dbl(lags, ~ median(unlist(nbdists(.x, st_coordinates(centres)))) / 1000),
                   moran_i = corr$res[, 1],
                   p = 2 * pnorm(-abs((corr$res[, 1] - corr$res[, 2]) / sqrt(corr$res[, 3]))))
corr_tab %>%
  mutate(distance_km = round(distance_km), moran_i = round(moran_i, 2),
         p = format.pval(p, eps = 0.001, digits = 2)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Order of neighbours", "Median distance, km", "Moran's I", "p-value"))
```

::: {.read}
**Clustering reaches about `r round(corr_tab$distance_km[4], -1)` km and then fades.** Moran's I is highest for the nearest townships (`r sprintf('%.2f', corr_tab$moran_i[1])`) and drops with each order, but stays significant up to order 4, about `r round(corr_tab$distance_km[4], -1)` km away. At order 5 it is close to zero, and at order 6 it is slightly negative, because townships that far apart are on opposite sides of a cluster. The 8 nearest neighbours are a median of `r round(corr_tab$distance_km[1])` km away, well inside this range, so each township is compared with places that share its level of conflict. A much wider neighbourhood would merge separate clusters. The next step finds where the clusters are.
:::

## Step 3. Clusters and outliers, local Moran's I

::: {.qcard}
Question
:   Which townships sit in a cluster of high or low conflict, and which are outliers, high among low or low among high?

Method, and why
:   Local Moran's I, `local_moran()` from **sfdep** (Anselin, 1995). It breaks global Moran's I into one value per township, so it finds both clusters and outliers, which the first objective asks for.

Null model
:   Conditional permutation. Each township's own count is held fixed while the counts of the other townships are shuffled 999 times.

Assumptions
:   The 8 nearest townships are the right comparison group. Counts are not rates, so a busy town may look high because more happens there.

Settings
:   Total events, row-standardised weights, 999 permutations, p < 0.05 from the permutation p-value (`p_ii_sim`). The quadrant uses the mean, as in the course. A median split is tested in Step 6.
:::

```{r}
#| filename: "local Moran's I"
set.seed(1234)
lisa <- wm_knn %>%
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(total, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran) %>%
  mutate(quadrant = if_else(p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Not significant"),
         quadrant = factor(quadrant, levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High", "Not significant")))

lisa %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(quadrant, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("LISA class", "Townships"))
```

::: {.read}
**The Dry Zone is one large cluster, and no busy township stands alone.** For `r nrow(lq) - nq("Not significant")` townships the null hypothesis of random placement is rejected at p < 0.05. `r nq("High-High")` are High-High, busy townships with busy neighbours, and `r nqs("High-High", dz)` of them form one block across Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay, around Monywa, Shwebo, Myaing and Pakokku. A smaller High-High group of `r nqs("High-High", "Tanintharyi")` sits around Dawei in Tanintharyi. Hakha in Chin, Shwegyin in Bago (East) and Kyaukme in northern Shan are single High-High townships. `r nq("Low-Low")` townships are Low-Low, in Yangon (`r nqs("Low-Low", "Yangon")`), the Ayeyarwady delta (`r nqs("Low-Low", "Ayeyarwady")`), Shan (East) (`r nqs("Low-Low", "Shan (East)")`), southern Shan and around Nay Pyi Taw. No township is a High-Low outlier, a busy township among quiet neighbours. The `r nq("Low-High")` Low-High outliers are quieter townships at the edge of hot areas, such as Nyaung-U and Seikphyu next to the Dry Zone block. They may be safer places, or places where events go unreported, but Step 6 shows they are the least stable result. A high count alone does not make a cluster. Kawkareik in Kayin, the second busiest township, is not significant because six of its eight nearest neighbours are quiet townships in Mon.
:::

### The Moran scatterplot behind the map

The LISA map comes from a Moran scatterplot, as in chapter 10 of the course text (Kam, 2026d). Each point is a township. The horizontal axis is its own standardised count. The vertical axis is the average standardised count of its 8 neighbours, its spatial lag from `st_lag()`. The four quarters of the plot are the four LISA classes. Coloured points are significant.

::: panel-tabset

```{r}
  mutate(z_total = as.vector(scale(total)),
```

## Step 4. Hot and cold spots, Getis-Ord Gi\*

::: {.qcard}
Question
:   Where do whole neighbourhoods carry far more conflict than chance, and where far less?

Method, and why
:   Getis-Ord Gi\*, `local_gstar_perm()` from **sfdep** (Getis and Ord, 1992; Ord and Getis, 1995). Unlike local Moran's I, it includes the township itself, so it measures a whole neighbourhood. EHSA in Task 3 is also built on Gi\*.

Null model
:   The same conditional permutation, 999 shuffles.

Assumptions
:   As for local Moran's I. Gi\* finds hot and cold spots but not outliers.

Settings
:   Total events, 8 nearest neighbours plus the township itself, row-standardised weights, two-sided permutation p-value (`p_sim`) as in the course, p < 0.05. A significant township is a hot spot when its Gi\* is positive and a cold spot when it is negative, as the lecture defines them. The hands-on code uses the `cluster` column instead, but that column only says whether the township itself is above average. For a few significant townships it disagrees with the sign of Gi\* and would turn hot neighbourhoods into cold spots, so the lecture rule is used.
:::

```{r}
#| filename: "local Gi*"
set.seed(1234)
hcsa <- wm_gi %>%
  mutate(local_gi = local_gstar_perm(total, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_gi) %>%
  mutate(spot = case_when(p_sim < 0.01 & gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot, p < 0.01",
                          p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot, p < 0.05",
                          p_sim < 0.01 & gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot, p < 0.01",
                          p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot, p < 0.05",
                          TRUE ~ "Not significant"),
         spot = factor(spot, levels = c("Hot spot, p < 0.01", "Hot spot, p < 0.05", "Cold spot, p < 0.05",
                                        "Cold spot, p < 0.01", "Not significant")))

hcsa %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(spot, .drop = FALSE) %>% kable(col.names = c("Gi* class", "Townships"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
hq <- hcsa %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% mutate(hot = str_detect(spot, "Hot"), cold = str_detect(spot, "Cold"))
hot_share <- sum(hq$total[hq$hot]) / sum(hq$total)
n_disagree <- sum(hq$p_sim < 0.05 & ((hq$gi_star > 0) != (hq$cluster == "High")))
```

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Getis-Ord Gi* of total armed conflict events, significant townships only (p < 0.05). Data from ACLED and MIMU"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| echo: false
gi_cols <- c("Hot spot, p < 0.01" = "#B2400B", "Hot spot, p < 0.05" = "#F1A26B",
             "Cold spot, p < 0.05" = "#8FBCE0", "Cold spot, p < 0.01" = "#0B5A99", "Not significant" = col_ns)

tm_shape(hcsa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "spot",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = gi_cols, levels.drop = TRUE),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Gi* class", position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"), frame = FALSE),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.2) +
  state_borders + state_names +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE) +
  tm_title(paste0(sum(hq$hot), " hot spot townships hold ", round(100 * hot_share), " percent of all events"),
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

```
:::

::: {.read}
**Hot spots cover a small area but hold nearly a third of all events.** `r sum(hq$hot)` townships are hot spots, `r sum(hq$spot == "Hot spot, p < 0.01")` of them at p < 0.01, and together they hold `r f_pct(hot_share)` of all events. `r sum(hq$hot & hq$ST %in% dz)` of them are in the Dry Zone, and the Sagaing part alone holds `r f_pct(sum(hq$total[hq$hot & hq$ST == "Sagaing"]) / sum(hq$total))` of all events. The rest are small groups around Dawei in Tanintharyi (`r sum(hq$hot & hq$ST == "Tanintharyi")`), Hakha in Chin (`r sum(hq$hot & hq$ST == "Chin")`), and single townships in Kayin and northern Shan. The hot spots are nearly the same townships as the High-High cluster, so the two statistics agree. `r sum(hq$cold)` townships are cold spots, mostly Yangon (`r sum(hq$cold & hq$ST == "Yangon")`), the Ayeyarwady delta (`r sum(hq$cold & hq$ST == "Ayeyarwady")`) and Shan (East) and (South) (`r sum(hq$cold & hq$ST %in% c("Shan (East)", "Shan (South)"))`). Busy townships elsewhere, such as Kawkareik, Hpakant and Kyaukkyi, are not hot spots because their neighbours are quieter. They are local flashpoints, not part of a wider hot area. Using the hands-on `cluster` column would have given `r n_disagree` significant townships the wrong label, all of them quieter townships inside hot neighbourhoods.
:::

## Step 5. Clusters by type of conflict

The total can hide differences between types, so local Moran's I and Gi\* are run again for each type with the same settings.

```{r}
#| filename: "local Moran's I and Gi* for each type"
lmsa_types <- map_dfr(c("battles", "remote", "civilians"), function(v) {
  set.seed(1234)
  lm_v <- local_moran(wm_knn[[v]], wm_knn$nb, wm_knn$wt, nsim = 999)
  set.seed(1234)
  gi_v <- local_gstar_perm(wm_gi[[v]], wm_gi$nb, wm_gi$wt, nsim = 999)
  mmr_conflict %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) %>%
    mutate(type = var_names[[v]],
           quadrant = if_else(lm_v$p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(lm_v$mean), "Not significant"),
           spot = case_when(gi_v$p_sim < 0.05 & gi_v$gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
                            gi_v$p_sim < 0.05 & gi_v$gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
                            TRUE ~ "Not significant"))
}) %>%
  mutate(type = factor(type, levels = var_names[c("battles", "remote", "civilians")]),
         quadrant = factor(quadrant, levels = names(lisa_cols)),
         spot = factor(spot, levels = c("Hot spot", "Cold spot", "Not significant")))

lmsa_types %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(type, quadrant, .drop = FALSE) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = quadrant, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  left_join(lmsa_types %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(type, spot, .drop = FALSE) %>%
              pivot_wider(names_from = spot, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>% select(-`Not significant`),
            by = "type") %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Type", "High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High", "Not significant (LISA)",
                      "Gi* hot spots", "Gi* cold spots"))
```

**Every type clusters in the Dry Zone, and each has a different second cluster.** All three types have a High-High cluster and a block of Gi\* hot spots in the Dry Zone. Battles are the most widespread, with `r ntp("battles", "spot", "Hot spot")` hot spots including groups around Myitkyina and Mohnyin in Kachin, in Kayah, and down Tanintharyi, where ethnic armed groups fight the military for territory. Explosions and remote violence have the fewest hot spots, `r ntp("remote", "spot", "Hot spot")`, with a second group where Bago (East) meets Kayin, around Shwegyin, Nyaunglebin and Hpa-An. Violence against civilians has `r ntp("civilians", "spot", "Hot spot")` hot spots, almost all in the Dry Zone and Tanintharyi. It also has the only High-Low outlier under the mean split, Pathein in the Ayeyarwady delta, which had more attacks on civilians than its quiet neighbours. The cold areas are the same for all three types. Because the second clusters differ by type, Bonus 1 looks at the mix of types directly.
:::

## Step 6. How much to trust these maps

Three checks test whether the maps depend on choices made above.

- **Many tests.** Testing 330 townships at p < 0.05 would flag about 16 by chance alone. `p.adjust()` with the false discovery rate (FDR) method (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) counts how many results survive.
- **Neighbour rule.** Local Moran's I is rerun with queen contiguity, with each island linked to its nearest township so that none is left out.
- **Mean or median.** Counts are skewed, so "high" and "low" are re-cut at the median instead of the mean.

```{r}
#| filename: "robustness checks"
fdr_tab <- tibble(
  map = c("Local Moran's I, total", "Gi*, total"),
  p_below_05 = c(sum(lisa$p_ii_sim < 0.05), sum(hcsa$p_sim < 0.05)),
  still_after_fdr = c(sum(p.adjust(lisa$p_ii_sim, "fdr") < 0.05), sum(p.adjust(hcsa$p_sim, "fdr") < 0.05)))
fdr_tab %>% kable(col.names = c("Map", "Significant at p < 0.05", "Still significant after FDR"))

nb_queen_fix <- nb_queen
iso <- which(spdep::card(nb_queen) == 0)
nn1 <- st_knn(centres, k = 1)
for (i in iso) {
  j <- nn1[[i]]
  nb_queen_fix[[i]] <- j
  nb_queen_fix[[j]] <- sort(unique(c(nb_queen_fix[[j]][nb_queen_fix[[j]] != 0], i)))
}
set.seed(1234)
lisa_q <- local_moran(mmr_conflict$total, nb_queen_fix, st_weights(nb_queen_fix), nsim = 999)
quad_q <- if_else(lisa_q$p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(lisa_q$mean), "Not significant")
quad_med <- if_else(lisa$p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(lisa$median), "Not significant")

tibble(class = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High"),
       main = map_int(class, ~ sum(lisa$quadrant == .x)),
       queen = map_int(class, ~ sum(quad_q == .x)),
       queen_same = map_int(class, ~ sum(quad_q == .x & lisa$quadrant == .x)),
       median = map_int(class, ~ sum(quad_med == .x))) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("LISA class", "Main result", "Queen contiguity", "Same township in both", "Median split"))

lisa %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(quad_med == "High-Low") %>% select(TS, ST, total) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("High-Low under the median split", "State or region", "Events"))
```

::: {.read}
**The main clusters hold, and the outliers are less certain.** After the FDR correction, `r fdr_tab$still_after_fdr[1]` of `r fdr_tab$p_below_05[1]` local Moran's I results and `r fdr_tab$still_after_fdr[2]` of `r fdr_tab$p_below_05[2]` Gi\* results remain, so most of the pattern is not caused by running many tests. Under queen contiguity, `r sum(quad_q == "High-High" & lisa$quadrant == "High-High")` of the `r nq("High-High")` High-High townships keep their class, and no township switches between high and low. The Dry Zone cluster is the same under both rules. The other classes change more. Low-Low townships fall from `r nq("Low-Low")` to `r sum(quad_q == "Low-Low")`, and only `r sum(quad_q == "Low-High" & lisa$quadrant == "Low-High")` of the `r nq("Low-High")` Low-High outliers keep their class. An outlier depends on which townships count as its neighbours, so it is most affected by that choice. The median split also affects outliers. A few very busy townships pull the mean up, so under the mean split Thaketa counts as "low". Against the median it is a little busier than usual and becomes a High-Low outlier. Since its label depends on the cut-off, Thaketa is a borderline case, not a clear flashpoint.
:::

```{r}
          "data/rds/results_lmsa.rds")
```

# Task 3. Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

Task 3 answers Q3 and the brief's second objective. Task 2 showed where conflict clustered over the whole period. Task 3 looks at how those clusters changed from quarter to quarter.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Short answer
The hot core stayed where it was, and conflict spread around it. The Sagaing core was a hot spot in most quarters but had no steady trend, so it does not appear on the trend map. The new and growing hot spots are around it. Five townships became hot late and stayed hot, in the hills of Bago (East) and on the road from Mandalay to northern Shan. Twenty-nine more changed from cold to hot, in Tanintharyi, Mon, central Rakhine, Bago (East) and the southern Dry Zone. Yangon cooled steadily, and northern Shan cooled sharply after the ceasefire in early 2024. Each type of violence spread in a different direction. The military's air strikes grew most in the Dry Zone and on the new fronts.
:::

## Step 1. Neighbours and weights in the cube

The 8 nearest neighbours from Task 2, plus the township itself, are added to the cube. `set_nbs()` and `set_wts()` copy them to every quarter, so every quarter uses the same neighbours. The course example in chapter 11 uses queen contiguity with inverse distance weights (Kam, 2026d). This report keeps the Task 2 neighbours instead, for two reasons. A hot spot then means the same thing in both tasks, so the results can be compared. And contiguity would leave three islands with no neighbour. Chapter 10 of the course text builds Gi\* weights from nearest neighbours in the same way.

```{r}
#| filename: "neighbours and weights in the cube"
conflict_nb <- conflict_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_knn(st_point_on_surface(geometry), k = 8)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")
```

## Step 2. Gi\* for every quarter, and the Mann-Kendall test

As in the course, Gi\* is computed for total events in each quarter with `local_gstar_perm()`, so each township has a series of 19 Gi\* values. Task 3 uses 199 permutations instead of 999, because Gi\* is computed for 19 quarters and, in Step 3, for five variables. The course text uses 99. With 199 the smallest possible p-value is 0.005, well below 0.05. The Mann-Kendall test, `MannKendall()` from **Kendall**, tests whether a series rises or falls more consistently than chance would give. Its tau goes from −1, always falling, to +1, always rising. The null hypothesis is that there is no monotonic trend.

```{r}
#| filename: "Gi* by quarter and the Mann-Kendall test for each township"
set.seed(1234)
gi_stars <- conflict_nb %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  mutate(gi_star = local_gstar_perm(total, nb, wt, nsim = 199)) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(gi_star) %>%
  ungroup()

mk <- gi_stars %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
  summarise(mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk) %>%
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(mmr_ts) %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST), by = "TS_PCODE")

mk %>% filter(sl < 0.05) %>%
  mutate(direction = if_else(tau > 0, "Rising", "Falling")) %>%
  count(direction, ST) %>%
  group_by(direction) %>% arrange(desc(n), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(townships = sum(n), led_by = paste0(head(ST, 4), " (", head(n, 4), ")", collapse = ", ")) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Significant trend", "Townships", "Led by"))
```

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-mk
#| fig-cap: "Gi* of total events by quarter for the township with the strongest significant rise and the one with the strongest significant fall. Data from ACLED and MIMU"
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 9
#| echo: false
pair <- bind_rows(mk %>% filter(sl < 0.05) %>% slice_max(tau, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE),
                  mk %>% filter(sl < 0.05) %>% slice_min(tau, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)) %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(TS, ", ", ST, "\n", if_else(tau > 0, "rising", "falling"), ", tau ", sprintf("%.2f", tau)))
pair_series <- gi_stars %>% filter(TS_PCODE %in% pair$TS_PCODE) %>%
  left_join(pair %>% select(TS_PCODE, label), by = "TS_PCODE")

# warm for the township heating up, blue for the one cooling down, labelled at the line ends instead of a legend
ggplot(pair_series, aes(time, gi_star, colour = label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = filter(pair_series, time == 19), aes(label = label), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.4,
            size = 4, fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c(col_high, col_low), pair$label), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 9, 13, 17), labels = c("2021", "2022", "2023", "2024", "2025"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.32))) +
  labs(title = "Mann-Kendall picks up steady change, not single spikes",
       subtitle = "Dashed lines mark Gi* of plus and minus 1.96, roughly the 5 percent level",
       x = NULL, y = "Gi* of total events") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## The Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| ref.label: "fig-mk"
```
:::

::: {.read}
**The test measures direction of change, not how hot a township is.** `r pair$TS[1]` in `r pair$ST[1]` has the strongest rise of all 330 townships. Its Gi\* started below −1.5, a cold neighbourhood, and rose in most quarters until it passed the hot spot line in early 2025. `r pair$TS[2]`, across the river from Yangon city, did the opposite, falling slowly from slightly above zero to near −2. Neither was a strong hot or cold spot for most of the period, but both trends are clear, with p well below 0.001. Across the country, `r sum(mk$sl < 0.05 & mk$tau > 0)` townships have a significant rise and `r sum(mk$sl < 0.05 & mk$tau < 0)` a significant fall. The largest groups of rising townships are in Bago (West) and Bago (East), where Okpho is, and Yangon has the most falling ones. Gi\* is measured against the whole country each quarter, so a falling Gi\* means a neighbourhood has a smaller share of the conflict, not that it is at peace.
:::

## Step 3. Emerging hot spot classes

`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` from **sfdep** (Parry, 2023) repeats the Gi\* step with a time lag, so the neighbours' values in the previous quarter also count. It runs the Mann-Kendall test on that series and gives each township one of the patterns in the Lesson 5 notes. It is run five times, once for each conflict variable and once for the military's air strikes. `include_gi = TRUE` keeps the quarterly Gi\* values so they can be checked.

```{r}
#| filename: "EHSA for every conflict variable"
ehsa_vars <- c(total = "All armed conflict", battles = "Battles",
               remote = "Explosions and remote violence", civilians = "Violence against civilians",
               military_air = "Military air strikes")
run_ehsa <- function(v) {
  set.seed(1234)
  e <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(conflict_nb, .var = v, k = 1, nsim = 199, threshold = 0.05,
                                 nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt", include_gi = TRUE)
  gi <- bind_cols(conflict_nb %>% as_tibble() %>% select(TS_PCODE, time),
                  attr(e, "gi_star") %>% as_tibble() %>% select(gi_star, p_sim))
  list(ehsa = as_tibble(e), gi = gi)
}
ehsa_all <- map(names(ehsa_vars), run_ehsa) %>% set_names(names(ehsa_vars))
```

### A check that each result sits on the right township

`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` labels its results in the row order of the boundary file, but calculates them in alphabetical order of township code. The two only match when the boundary is sorted by code. A first run without sorting put cold spots over Sagaing, the most violent area in @fig-total, which showed the problem. This is why `mmr_ts` was sorted in Task 1. Two checks confirm the fix. Re-running the Mann-Kendall test on the saved Gi\* series must give exactly sfdep's tau. And sfdep's tau should be close to the Step 2 tau, which uses the same counts without the time lag.

```{r}
#| filename: "check that EHSA results line up with townships"
own <- ehsa_all$total$gi %>% arrange(TS_PCODE, time) %>% group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
  summarise(tau_own = Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)$tau[1])
chk <- ehsa_all$total$ehsa %>% select(TS_PCODE = location, tau) %>%
  left_join(own, by = "TS_PCODE") %>% left_join(mk %>% select(TS_PCODE, tau_step2 = tau), by = "TS_PCODE")
tibble(check = c("Largest gap between sfdep's tau and the re-run tau",
                 "Correlation with the Step 2 tau (no time lag)"),
       value = c(signif(max(abs(chk$tau - chk$tau_own)), 2), round(cor(chk$tau, chk$tau_step2), 2))) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Check", "Value"))
```

The gap is zero, so every result belongs to the right township. The correlation with Step 2 is high but not perfect, as expected, because EHSA also uses the previous quarter's values.

### A check against the lecture definitions

sfdep's source code has two rules that differ from the definitions in the Lesson 5 notes, and there is one case where the lecture definitions overlap.

| Pattern | Lecture definition | sfdep rule | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sporadic hot or cold spot | Must be significant in the **final** quarter | Does not check the final quarter | Fading townships are labelled sporadic |
| Intensifying hot spot | Hot in at least 90 percent of quarters | Significant in 90 percent of quarters, hot **or cold** | A cold spot that is warming can be labelled an intensifying hot spot |
| Consecutive and oscillating hot spot | A township that was cold, then hot to the end, fits both definitions | Calls it oscillating. It only calls a township consecutive if it was never significant, hot or cold, before its final hot run | The lecture gives no order, so sfdep's choice is kept and applied to every township |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,26,30,26]"}

The report keeps sfdep's classes but corrects the first two cases with the lecture rules, applied to sfdep's own Gi\* values. `lecture_class()` below codes the lecture tables, and follows sfdep's order where they overlap.

```{r}
#| filename: "lecture definitions, applied to sfdep's own Gi* values"
lecture_class <- function(gs, sig, tau, tau_p, alpha = 0.05) {
  n <- length(gs); hot <- sig & gs > 0; cold <- sig & gs < 0
  final_run <- function(x) { r <- rle(x); if (!tail(r$values, 1)) 0 else tail(r$lengths, 1) }
  if (hot[n]) {
    before <- hot[seq_len(n - final_run(hot))]
    if (sum(hot) == 1) return("New hotspot")
    if (final_run(hot) >= 2 && !any(sig[seq_len(n - final_run(hot))]) && mean(hot) < 0.9) return("Consecutive hotspot")
    if (mean(hot) >= 0.9) return(if (tau_p >= alpha) "Persistent hotspot" else if (tau > 0) "Intensifying hotspot" else "Diminishing hotspot")
    return(if (any(cold)) "Oscillating hotspot" else "Sporadic hotspot")
  }
  if (cold[n]) {
    before <- cold[seq_len(n - final_run(cold))]
    if (sum(cold) == 1) return("New coldspot")
    if (final_run(cold) >= 2 && !any(sig[seq_len(n - final_run(cold))]) && mean(cold) < 0.9) return("Consecutive coldspot")
    if (mean(cold) >= 0.9) return(if (tau_p >= alpha) "Persistent coldspot" else if (tau < 0) "Intensifying coldspot" else "Diminishing coldspot")
    return(if (any(hot)) "Oscillating coldspot" else "Sporadic coldspot")
  }
  if (mean(hot) >= 0.9) return("Historical hotspot")
  if (mean(cold) >= 0.9) return("Historical coldspot")
  "No pattern detected"
}

classify <- function(res) {
  series <- res$gi %>% arrange(TS_PCODE, time) %>% group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
    summarise(gs = list(gi_star), sig = list(p_sim < 0.05),
              hot_q = sum(gi_star > 0 & p_sim < 0.05), cold_q = sum(gi_star < 0 & p_sim < 0.05))
  res$ehsa %>% rename(TS_PCODE = location) %>%
    left_join(series, by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
    mutate(sfdep_class = str_to_sentence(str_replace(classification, "oscilating", "oscillating")),
           final_hot = map_lgl(gs, ~ .x[length(.x)] > 0) & map_lgl(sig, ~ .x[length(.x)]),
           final_cold = map_lgl(gs, ~ .x[length(.x)] < 0) & map_lgl(sig, ~ .x[length(.x)]),
           pattern = case_when(
             sfdep_class == "Sporadic hotspot" & !final_hot ~ "No pattern detected",
             sfdep_class == "Sporadic coldspot" & !final_cold ~ "No pattern detected",
             sfdep_class == "Intensifying hotspot" & hot_q / 19 < 0.9 ~ pmap_chr(list(gs, sig, tau, p_value), lecture_class),
             TRUE ~ sfdep_class)) %>%
    select(-gs, -sig)
}
ehsa_tab <- map_dfr(names(ehsa_vars), ~ classify(ehsa_all[[.x]]) %>% mutate(variable = ehsa_vars[[.x]]))

ehsa_tab %>% filter(p_value < 0.05, sfdep_class != pattern) %>%
  count(variable, sfdep_class, pattern) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Variable", "sfdep class", "Corrected class", "Townships"))
```

Most corrections move "sporadic" townships that were not significant in the final quarter to "No pattern detected". The table also shows two townships in Shan that sfdep called intensifying hot spots for explosions and remote violence. They were cold spots in almost every quarter and slowly warming, which the lecture calls diminishing cold spots.

## Step 4. Where hot spots are emerging

The brief asks for EHSA maps that show only townships with a significant Mann-Kendall trend (p < 0.05). This rule leaves out one kind of township. A township that is hot in nearly every quarter has no trend, so it never passes the filter. So the trend map is shown next to a second map of how many of the 19 quarters each township was a significant hot spot.

```{r}
#| echo: false

                 "Diminishing hotspot", "Oscillating hotspot", "Sporadic hotspot", "Historical hotspot",
```

::: {.read}
**Most townships changed on and off rather than steadily.** Of the `r n_sig_tot` townships with a significant trend in all conflict, `r nb_cls("No pattern detected")` fit none of the named patterns, mostly because they were not significant in the final quarter, which nearly every named pattern requires. `r n_moved` of these were moved from sfdep's sporadic class by the lecture-rule check in Step 3. The next largest groups are oscillating hot spots (`r nb_cls("Oscillating hotspot")`) and oscillating cold spots (`r nb_cls("Oscillating coldspot")`), townships that changed from cold to hot or from hot to cold. Only `r nb_cls("Consecutive hotspot")` townships became hot and stayed hot, and none is a new, intensifying or persistent hot spot. This is what a war with moving front lines looks like, because Gi\* compares each township with the rest of the country in the same quarter, and the rest of the country keeps changing. The other variables are similar, except that sporadic cold spots are a large group for explosions (`r nb_cls("Sporadic coldspot", "Explosions")`) and air strikes (`r nb_cls("Sporadic coldspot", "Air strikes")`). These townships were cold now and then and never hot. Across all five variables there is one new hot spot, Hpakant for explosions. The maps below show where each class is.
:::

::: {.read}
**The core stayed hot, and conflict spread around it.** `r nrow(sig_tot)` of 330 townships have a significant trend, a few more than the `r sum(mk$sl < 0.05)` in Step 2, because EHSA's Gi\* also uses the previous quarter. The right map explains why the Sagaing core is mostly blank on the left. Its High-High townships were significant hot spots in `r core_q[1]` to `r core_q[2]` of the 19 quarters. Their Gi\* rose to a peak in 2023 and then fell, so there is no single direction and no significant trend. The growing hot spots are around the core. `r np("Consecutive hotspot")` consecutive hot spots, which became hot late and stayed hot, are in the hills of Bago (East) and on the road from Mandalay to northern Shan. `r np("Oscillating hotspot")` oscillating hot spots, cold earlier and hot by the end, are in Tanintharyi, Mon, central Rakhine, Bago (East) and the south of the Dry Zone. On the cold side, `r sum(sig_tot$ST == "Yangon" & str_detect(sig_tot$pattern, "coldspot"))` of Yangon's `r sum(tot$ST == "Yangon")` townships are in a cold pattern. Six townships on the northern Shan border were the hottest in the country in late 2023 and became cold afterwards. Each pattern is described below.
:::

### Reading each pattern

**Consecutive hot spots, `r np("Consecutive hotspot")` townships.** These are the clearest new hot spots. `r paste(sig_tot$TS[sig_tot$pattern == "Consecutive hotspot"], collapse = ", ")` were not hot in 2021 but became hot and stayed hot to the end, with Gi\* rising from about zero to between 3 and 7. They are on two new fronts. One is the hills of Bago (East) next to Kayin, around Kyaukkyi and Shwegyin. The other is the road from Mandalay to northern Shan, through Mogoke, Nawnghkio and Kyaukme, where fighting moved in the second phase of Operation 1027 in 2024. Both run from the border areas towards the centre of the country, so this is where the conflict is still moving.

**Oscillating hot spots, `r np("Oscillating hotspot")` townships.** This is the largest hot pattern. Each township was a significant cold spot at least once, usually in 2021, and is hot in the final quarter. There are four groups. `r np("Oscillating hotspot", "Tanintharyi")` cover most of Tanintharyi, from Dawei to Kawthoung. `r np("Oscillating hotspot", "Rakhine")` are in central Rakhine, around Kyaukpyu and Ramree, which were cold in 2021 and turned hot in 2024 as fighting moved south through the state. `r np("Oscillating hotspot", "Mon")` are in Mon and `r np("Oscillating hotspot", "Bago (East)")` in Bago (East). The rest are in the Dry Zone, mostly in the south around Myingyan, Taungtha, Chauk and Salin, plus Singu on the road to northern Shan. Conflict reached all of these places during the study period.

**Sporadic hot spots, `r np("Sporadic hotspot")` townships.** These are hot in the final quarter and were hot on and off before, but never cold. `r np("Sporadic hotspot", "Kayin")` are in Kayin, including Kawkareik, Myawaddy and Hpa-An on the Thai border. Their Gi\* was highest in 2025, so fighting on the south-east border is increasing again.

**Oscillating cold spots, `r np("Oscillating coldspot")` townships.** These were hot at least once and are cold now. `r np("Oscillating coldspot", "Shan (North)")` are on the Chinese border in northern Shan, including Laukkaing, Hseni and Kunlong. They were the hottest places in Myanmar in late 2023, when Operation 1027 began (the spike in @fig-ehsa-series), and became cold after the ceasefire brokered by China in early 2024. The other `r np("Oscillating coldspot") - np("Oscillating coldspot", "Shan (North)")` are in Yangon and around Mandalay city. They were briefly hot during the urban resistance of 2021 and have been cold since.

**Intensifying, consecutive and sporadic cold spots, `r np("Intensifying coldspot") + np("Consecutive coldspot") + np("Sporadic coldspot")` townships.** The `r np("Intensifying coldspot")` intensifying cold spots are all in Yangon, including downtown Pazundaung, Botahtaung and Kyauktada, and they grow colder each year. Thingangyun and Hlaing are consecutive cold spots. The sporadic cold spots are mostly in Yangon and the delta. Together they show conflict declining in Myanmar's largest city.

**No pattern detected, `r np("No pattern detected")` townships.** These have a significant trend but fit none of the patterns, usually because they were not significant in the final quarter. There are two groups. `r sum(sig_tot$pattern == "No pattern detected" & sig_tot$tau < 0)` are falling, led by Chin, Kachin, Mandalay and the north-west of Sagaing, where conflict peaked in 2021 or 2022 and faded. `r sum(sig_tot$pattern == "No pattern detected" & sig_tot$tau > 0)` are rising, `r sum(sig_tot$pattern == "No pattern detected" & sig_tot$tau > 0 & sig_tot$ST == "Bago (West)")` of them in Bago (West), including Okpho from @fig-mk. They are warming but are not yet hot spots, so they are the townships to watch.

```{r}
#| echo: false
npt <- function(v, p, s = NULL) sum(et$variable == v & et$p_value < 0.05 & et$pattern == p & (is.null(s) | et$ST %in% s))
nsig <- function(v) sum(et$variable == v & et$p_value < 0.05)
tsn <- function(v, p, s = NULL) paste(et$TS[et$variable == v & et$p_value < 0.05 & et$pattern == p & (is.null(s) | et$ST %in% s)], collapse = ", ")
```

**Battles, `r nsig("Battles")` townships with a significant trend.** Ground fighting moved to the coast and the far south. `r npt("Battles", "Oscillating hotspot")` townships changed from cold to hot, led by Tanintharyi (`r npt("Battles", "Oscillating hotspot", "Tanintharyi")`) and central Rakhine (`r npt("Battles", "Oscillating hotspot", "Rakhine")`). `r npt("Battles", "Oscillating coldspot", "Shan (North)")` northern Shan townships were hot during Operation 1027 and cold after the 2024 ceasefire. Only about half of the battle trends pass the false discovery rate check in Step 7, so this map is less certain than the others.

**Explosions and remote violence, `r nsig("Explosions and remote violence")` townships.** Explosions spread into the hills between the Dry Zone and Kayin, and into the south. `r npt("Explosions and remote violence", "Oscillating hotspot")` townships changed from cold to hot, led by Tanintharyi (`r npt("Explosions and remote violence", "Oscillating hotspot", "Tanintharyi")`) and Bago (East) (`r npt("Explosions and remote violence", "Oscillating hotspot", "Bago (East)")`). Hpakant is a new hot spot. Yangon and the delta became colder as the bombings of 2021 and 2022 stopped.

**Violence against civilians, `r nsig("Violence against civilians")` townships.** This type shows the clearest move. `r npt("Violence against civilians", "Oscillating hotspot", "Bago (West)")` of its `r npt("Violence against civilians", "Oscillating hotspot")` oscillating hot spots are in Bago (West), including Letpadan and Okpho, an area with little fighting. The far north-west, around Kale and Tedim, changed from hot to cold. Attacks on civilians are moving south into the lowlands.

## Step 6. The military's air strikes

@fig-remote showed that the military's air strikes rose about 23-fold. Air strikes can reach any township, so they are mapped on their own.
